title: PT, APTT and the Mixing Study: Deficiency or Inhibitor?
summary: Light up the factors each screening test measures, then pour patient and normal plasma together and watch a shortage correct — while an inhibitor, fast or slow, keeps the APTT long.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 36 Hit 1 (core: mixing study), Hit 2 (PT and APTT factor coverage), Hit 8 (contact-factor deficiencies without bleeding), Trap 2 and the Figure 36 memory anchor. Checked against Santoro 2023 and the 2020 international acquired-hemophilia A recommendations. Not taught: factor XIII and the thrombin time (Hit 2) and the prekallikrein incubation effect (Hit 8), which remain pending.

objectives: Name the factors measured by PT and APTT and interpret isolated prolongation of each.
Explain why a 1:1 mix corrects a deficiency but not an inhibitor.
Use incubated mixing, the Rosner index and factor assays, and recognize prolonged APTTs without bleeding risk.

scenes.title: A long APTT before surgery
scenes.altText: A pre-operative screen: PT normal, APTT clearly prolonged (flagged). Two possible explanations appear as tokens: “Missing a clotting factor?” and “Something blocking the factors (an inhibitor)?”. A beaker labelled “normal pooled plasma” waits on the bench.

cues.text: A patient is screened before surgery. The PT is normal, but the APTT is clearly prolonged.
Two very different problems can do this: a missing clotting factor, or something in the plasma that blocks clotting — an inhibitor.
One simple test starts to tell them apart: mix the patient’s plasma with normal plasma and repeat the APTT.

scenes.title: Normal: what PT and APTT each test
scenes.altText: Two reagent lanes. PT: tissue factor is added to plasma; the lane lights up factors I (fibrinogen), II, V, VII and X. APTT: a contact activator (such as kaolin, silica or ellagic acid) plus phospholipid is added, then calcium; the lane lights up factors I, II, V, VIII, IX, X, XI and XII, plus the contact proteins prekallikrein and high-molecular-weight kininogen. Shared factors (I, II, V, X) glow in both lanes; factor VII is the only one in the PT lane alone.

cues.text: The PT adds tissue factor to the plasma. It mainly checks factors one, two, five, seven and ten.

The APTT adds a contact activator, such as kaolin or silica, with phospholipid, then calcium. It checks factors one, two, five, eight, nine, ten, eleven and twelve — plus prekallikrein and high-molecular-weight kininogen.
Factors one, two, five and ten appear in both tests. A shortage there can prolong both.
Factor seven appears only in the PT. So an isolated long PT points toward factor seven, and an isolated long APTT points toward eight, nine, eleven, twelve or the contact proteins — or an inhibitor.

props.label: In both: I, II, V, X (common)
Isolated long PT → VII · isolated long APTT → VIII, IX, XI, XII…

scenes.title: What changes when you mix 1:1
scenes.altText: Two tubes pour into a third: patient plasma and normal pooled plasma in equal volumes. Deficiency case: the patient tube shows few factor-VIII tokens, the normal pool many; the mix ends with about half the normal amount, enough for a normal APTT — a green “corrects” stamp. Inhibitor case: antibody tokens in the patient plasma attack factor tokens from the normal pool too; the mix stays prolonged — a red “does not correct” stamp.

cues.text: Mix the patient’s plasma one-to-one with normal pooled plasma — a pool from many healthy donors, with every factor near 100 percent.
If the patient is simply missing a factor, the mix contains about half the normal amount. Around 50 percent is enough for a normal APTT, so the APTT corrects.
If the patient has an inhibitor, the antibody attacks the factor from the normal plasma too. The APTT stays long: it does not correct.
So: corrects suggests a deficiency; does not correct suggests an inhibitor. That is the rule — but the next scene shows where it needs care.

props.label: Corrects → deficiency · does not correct → inhibitor

scenes.title: In the lab: time, temperature and the grey zone
scenes.altText: A timeline: mix → test immediately → incubate at 37 °C for 2 hours → test again (with the normal pool and patient plasma incubated separately as controls). An acquired-hemophilia FVIII autoantibody is shown working slowly: the immediate mix looks corrected, but after 2 hours the APTT is long again. A formula card: index of circulating anticoagulant (Rosner index) = (mix − normal pool) ÷ patient × 100, with a typical cut-off of 10–15% that depends on reagent and analyzer. A caution card: mixing tests are poorly standardized and cannot establish or exclude acquired hemophilia A — measure factor activities.

cues.text: Some inhibitors are slow. Autoantibodies against factor eight, in acquired hemophilia A, need time and body temperature to act.
So test the mix immediately and again after two hours at 37 degrees, incubating the normal pool and the patient’s plasma separately as controls.
A mix that corrects at first but prolongs after incubation points to a time-dependent inhibitor.

To make “corrects” less subjective, many labs calculate the Rosner index: mix minus normal pool, divided by patient, times 100. A cut-off around 10 to 15 percent is typical, but it depends on the reagent.
And mixing tests are poorly standardized. They can’t prove or exclude acquired hemophilia — measure factor eight and the other factor activities.

props.text: Controls: normal pool and patient plasma incubated separately

props.label: Poorly standardized → always measure factor activities

scenes.title: Two classic traps
scenes.altText: Trap card: “Very long APTT = high bleeding risk” is crossed out → “Factor XII, prekallikrein and HMW-kininogen deficiencies, and lupus anticoagulant, prolong the APTT without bleeding.” Trap card: “A mildly long APTT that corrects = factor deficiency” is crossed out → “A weak inhibitor can be diluted out by mixing; interpret with care.”

cues.text: Trap one: a very long APTT does not always mean bleeding. Deficiencies of factor twelve, prekallikrein or high-molecular-weight kininogen can prolong the APTT dramatically without causing bleeding. Lupus anticoagulant prolongs it too, and isn’t a bleeding risk.
Trap two: a mildly long APTT that corrects on mixing isn’t automatically a deficiency. A low-titre inhibitor can be diluted enough to look corrected.
And a mix that corrects immediately can still hide a slow inhibitor. Check the incubated mix and the factor levels.

props.title: ✗ “Very long APTT = high bleeding risk.”
lines: ✓ FXII, PK, HMWK deficiency and lupus anticoagulant: no bleeding

props.title: ✗ “Mild APTT that corrects = deficiency.”
lines: ✓ A weak inhibitor can be diluted out — interpret with care

props.label: Immediate correction ≠ no inhibitor → incubate 2 h

scenes.title: Half is enough
scenes.altText: Memory aid: a half-full fuel gauge labelled “50% is enough to clot” — a shortage is fixed by topping up; a saboteur (inhibitor) drains the new fuel too; a slow saboteur needs a 2-hour, 37 °C stake-out. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: half is enough. Topping up a shortage with normal plasma fixes it. A saboteur — an inhibitor — drains the new supply too. And slow saboteurs need a two-hour stake-out at 37 degrees.

Where it breaks: weak inhibitors can look fixed, lupus anticoagulants behave differently and need their own tests, and the cut-off for “corrected” depends on the reagent. Factor assays give the answer.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: Weak inhibitors can look corrected · lupus anticoagulant needs its own tests
“Corrected” cut-offs depend on the reagent · factor assays decide

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Three tokens: “PT: I, II, V, VII, X · APTT: I, II, V, VIII, IX, X, XI, XII”, “1:1 mix corrects → deficiency · no correction → inhibitor”, “Incubate 2 h at 37 °C for slow FVIII inhibitors; confirm with factor assays”.

cues.text: If a prolonged APTT corrects in a 1:1 mix with normal plasma, suspect a factor deficiency, and if it does not — or prolongs again after two hours at 37 degrees — suspect an inhibitor, then confirm with factor assays.

props.label: PT: I, II, V, VII, X · APTT: I, II, V, VIII, IX, X, XI, XII
1:1 mix corrects → deficiency · no correction → inhibitor
Incubate 2 h at 37 °C for slow FVIII inhibitors · factor assays

explanation.what: Plain language: the PT and APTT time how fast plasma clots after different triggers; a mixing study adds normal plasma to see whether something is missing or something is blocking. Scientific terms: PT (tissue factor) mainly reflects factors I, II, V, VII and X; APTT (contact activator + phospholipid, then calcium) reflects I, II, V, VIII, IX, X, XI and XII plus prekallikrein and HMW kininogen; a 1:1 mix with normal pooled plasma corrects a deficiency but not an inhibitor.
explanation.why: Normal pooled plasma has each factor near 100 U/dL, so a 1:1 mix provides about 50 U/dL, enough for a normal APTT even if the patient has none. An inhibitor neutralizes the normal plasma’s factor too. FVIII autoantibodies in acquired hemophilia A are time- and temperature-dependent, so the mix may correct immediately and prolong after 2 h at 37 °C.
explanation.measure: Immediate and incubated (37 °C, 2 h) 1:1 mixes, with incubated normal-pool and patient controls; the index of circulating anticoagulant (Rosner index) = (CTmix − CTNPP) ÷ CTpatient × 100, cut-off typically 10–15% depending on reagent; then specific factor activity assays. A 4:1 mix may help when inhibitors are weak.
explanation.differs: Deficiency (corrects) vs inhibitor (does not correct, or prolongs after incubation); bleeding causes of a long APTT (VIII, IX, XI deficiency, acquired hemophilia) vs non-bleeding causes (FXII, prekallikrein, HMWK deficiency, lupus anticoagulant).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: which factors PT and APTT detect, isolated long PT (FVII), interpretation of an immediate vs incubated mix, acquired hemophilia A, and the non-bleeding long APTT.

right.label: Inhibitor

mnemonic.text: Half is enough — a top-up fixes a shortage, not a saboteur.
mnemonic.explanation: A 1:1 mix gives about 50% of each factor, which normalizes the APTT in a deficiency; an inhibitor (saboteur) neutralizes the added factor; slow saboteurs (FVIII autoantibodies) need 2 h at 37 °C to show.
mnemonic.limitation: Weak inhibitors can be diluted out and look corrected; lupus anticoagulant needs dedicated tests; “corrected” cut-offs depend on reagent and analyzer; factor assays give the answer.

questions.stem: A patient has an isolated prolonged APTT. A 1:1 mix with normal pooled plasma corrects immediately, but after 2 hours at 37 °C the mix is prolonged again (incubated controls are normal). What is most likely?

options.text: A time-dependent factor VIII inhibitor, as in acquired hemophilia A
options.rationale: Correct. FVIII autoantibodies are time- and temperature-dependent; they may correct immediately and prolong after incubation.
Incorrect. A simple deficiency stays corrected after incubation when the controls are normal.
Incorrect. Factor VII deficiency prolongs the PT, not the APTT.
Incorrect. Like any deficiency, it stays corrected after incubation when the controls are normal.

questions.stem: Which result pattern points most specifically to factor VII deficiency?

options.text: Prolonged PT with a normal APTT
options.rationale: Correct. Factor VII is in the PT pathway only.

options.text: Prolonged APTT with a normal PT
options.rationale: Incorrect. That points to VIII, IX, XI, XII, the contact proteins or an inhibitor.
Incorrect. That suggests a common factor (I, II, V, X) or multiple deficiencies.
Incorrect. Factor VII deficiency prolongs the PT.

questions.stem: A healthy man with no bleeding history has a markedly prolonged APTT that corrects completely on mixing. Which deficiency best fits?

options.rationale: Correct. Contact-factor deficiencies (FXII, prekallikrein, HMWK) prolong the APTT without causing bleeding.
Incorrect. Severe hemophilia A causes bleeding.
Incorrect. An inhibitor would not correct completely, and acquired hemophilia usually presents with bleeding.
